title: Gram Staining

references.label: Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL)

purpose: To differentially stain bacteria based on cell wall composition, sorting them into Gram-positive and Gram-negative groups as a first step in identification.
principle: Gram-positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan layer that traps the crystal violet–iodine complex when dehydrated by decolorizer, retaining the purple stain. Gram-negative cells have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane that is disrupted by the decolorizer, releasing the crystal violet and allowing the counterstain (safranin) to color the cells pink/red.

procedure.instruction: Prepare a thin bacterial smear on a clean slide and air dry.
Heat-fix the smear by passing the slide briefly through a flame (smear side up), or use a methanol fixation alternative.
procedure.note: Heat-fixation kills most vegetative cells and adheres them to the slide; over-heating distorts morphology.

procedure.instruction: Flood the smear with crystal violet and let stand for about 1 minute, then rinse gently with water.
Flood with Gram's iodine and let stand for about 1 minute, then rinse gently with water.
procedure.note: Iodine forms a crystal violet-iodine complex within the cell.

procedure.instruction: Decolorize by adding decolorizer drop-wise until runoff is nearly clear (typically a few seconds) — this is the most technique-sensitive, timing-dependent step.
procedure.note: Over-decolorization can falsely stain Gram-positive cells as Gram-negative; under-decolorization can do the reverse.

procedure.instruction: Immediately rinse with water to stop decolorization.
Counterstain with safranin for about 30–60 seconds, then rinse with water.
Blot dry with bibulous paper (do not rub) and examine under oil immersion (1000×).

observations: Gram-positive organisms appear purple/violet. Gram-negative organisms appear pink/red. Note also cell shape (cocci, bacilli, spirilla) and arrangement (chains, clusters, pairs).
interpretation: Gram reaction is a first-tier identification character used alongside morphology, arrangement, and subsequent biochemical tests — it narrows, but does not by itself confirm, organism identity.
criticalNotes: Smear thickness matters: an overly thick smear can trap decolorizer and produce a false Gram-positive result.
Culture age matters: Gram-positive organisms in an aging culture can lose cell wall integrity and stain Gram-variable or falsely Gram-negative.
precautions: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious.
Handle flame/heat-fixation carefully around flammable reagents.
Dispose of stained slides and reagent waste per local biosafety procedure.
limitations: Some genera (e.g. Mycobacterium) do not Gram stain reliably due to a waxy cell wall and require acid-fast staining instead.
Very young or very old cultures may give inconsistent results.
biosafetyNotes: Use standard aseptic technique when preparing the smear from a live culture. Biosafety level depends on the organism being handled, not on the staining procedure itself.
